Minutes:
Before the officer’s presentation, members discussed the
arrangements for a technical briefing held prior to the committee meeting,
expressing concerns that the meeting had been arranged without consultation
with the Chair and Vice-Chair of the Committee and that ECC Highways had not
been invited to attend given the significance of the application. Members
emphasised the importance of transparency and ensuring appropriate stakeholder
involvement in future briefings. Officers and the Monitoring Officer clarified
that no decisions had been made at the briefing, explained that technical
briefings are intended to assist members by addressing technical questions and
noted that applications may be submitted for non-determination in accordance
with the statutory process. It was agreed that efforts should be made to secure
Highways representation at future meetings where highway matters are a
significant consideration.
The Committee considered an outline application for a large
residential-led development (up to 910 dwellings – 50% of which would be
affordable housing – and 8 Gypsy and Traveller pitches) on 56.9ha of Green Belt
land, currently in agricultural use, on the edge of Great Burstead. Land had
been set aside in the indicative layout for a three-form entry primary school.
It was noted that an appeal had been lodged on the grounds
of non-determination. The Committee was asked to indicate the decision it would
have made had the application remained with the Council for determination.
The S106 package, in excess of £20 million, included
contributions towards education, healthcare, culture, play and sports, bus
service enhancement, employment and skills, and Essex Coast RAMS plus
monitoring fees. Non-monetary contributions comprised 50% affordable housing,
eight Gypsy and Traveller pitches, 3.44ha land safeguarded for a school, and
environmental benefits.
The officer advised that, having undertaken the planning
balance exercise, the benefits of the proposal were considered to significantly
outweigh the identified Green Belt and other harms. It was concluded that very
special circumstances existed to justify the development, and it was noted that
no objections had been received from statutory consultees. Consequently, the
application was recommended for approval.

larger vehicles. Residents highlighted existing pressures on local schools, GP

1.1.1 This application seeks outline planning permission (with all matters reserved
 except access) for a residential-led mixed-use development on land at Foots
 Farm, Southend Road, Billericay. The proposal comprises up to 910 dwellings,
 including 50% affordable housing, a community hub (Class E), 8 Gypsy and
 Traveller pitches, approximately 3.44 hectares of safeguarded education land
 capable of accommodating a nursery and three-form entry primary school,
 extensive public open space, Suitable Alternative Natural Greenspace (SANG),
 sustainable drainage infrastructure, biodiversity enhancements and associated
 highway and transport improvements.

1.1.2 The site extends to approximately 56.89 hectares and lies within the Metropolitan
 Green Belt. Whilst officers conclude that the development would not
 fundamentally undermine the purposes of the remaining Green Belt across the
 wider plan area, the site is not identified as Grey Belt land within the Council's
 evidence base and the proposal therefore does not satisfy all of the requirements
 of NPPF Policy GB7. The proposal therefore constitutes inappropriate
 development in the Green Belt The development would result in harm to the
 Green Belt by reason of inappropriateness, together with harm to openness and
 conflict with Green Belt purposes. These harms attract substantial weight against

Minutes:
Members considered a full planning application for 16
dwellings, including 50% affordable housing. The affordable housing, plots 9 –
16 at the north end of the site, would comprise six affordable rent units and
two offered under a shared ownership scheme.
The application site, whilst located in the Green Belt, did
not make a strong contribution to the Green Belt purposes and could
appropriately be regarded as grey belt. It was located close to the Great
Burstead Conservation Area and adjacent to listed buildings. The access to
Burstead Grange, off Church Street, was included in the application site and
enhancements to the access road were proposed.
Members noted the update sheet (appended to these minutes)
including: a consultation response from Essex Fire and Rescue Sevice confirming
no objection; amendments to the wording of Condition 35, concerning access and
drainage arrangements, in response to a resident representation; an additional
objection from a resident who was unable to attend the meeting or speak
remotely.
The proposal included a monetary S106 contribution totalling
just under £30,000 plus monitoring fees, towards healthcare, open space,
culture, play and sports, employment and skills and waste and recycling. No
contribution towards education had been sought.
The Planning Officer advised that the proposal represented
development of a Grey Belt site in accordance with national planning policy and
would deliver benefits including new housing, 50% affordable housing, public
open space, enhancements to the public footpath network and high-quality design
and landscaping. It was noted that no statutory consultee had raised objections
that could not be addressed through planning conditions. Whilst acknowledging
some harm arising from the loss of open land, a change in character and a low
level of harm to the setting of the Grade II listed building, the officer
concluded that these impacts were outweighed by the benefits of the scheme and
therefore recommended approval.

density of the proposed development to be out of keeping with the semi-rural

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

1.1 This report describes the above planning application and sets out the officer’s
 assessment and recommended decision, having regard to the National Planning Policy
 Framework 2026, the Saved Basildon Local Plan, the emerging Basildon Local Plan and
 other material considerations.

1.2 The application seeks planning permission for the erection of 16 dwellings and
 associated landscaping and parking. The application is located in the Green Belt.

1.3 The key considerations are identified as being: the principle of developing this Green Belt
 site, whether the development would utilise Grey Belt land and whether any Very Special
 Circumstances apply; as well as matters of design, visual impact, impact upon heritage
 assets, impact upon amenity of neighbouring and future occupiers including
 considerations of noise, air quality and odour; highway safety matters; flood risk and
 drainage; water quality; ecology and biodiversity; designing out crime; and S106 Matters.

1.4 Officers conclude that the site does not make a strong contribution to the relevant Green
 Belt purposes identified in paragraph GB2 of the Revised NPPF and may appropriately
 be regarded as grey belt land. Accordingly, the proposal does not constitute inappropriate
 development within the Green Belt.

1.5 The proposed development would deliver 16 new dwellings, including 50% affordable
 housing. This benefit attracts significant weight in favour of the proposal, particularly in
 light of the Council’s acute housing land supply shortfall, currently standing at 41% of its
 requirement, equivalent to approximately 2.05 years’ supply, together with the identified
 unmet need for affordable housing across the Borough. The proposal also satisfies the
 Golden Rules set

[page 2]
over building scale, form and massing, the proposal would create a high-quality
 residential environment that sits comfortably within the wider landscape.

1.7 Officers acknowledge that the proposal would result in some harm, principally arising
 from the loss of undeveloped Green Belt land and a degree of change to landscape
 character and openness. However, this harm is moderated by the landscape-led design
 of the scheme, the retention of substantial open areas within the site and the overall
 pattern of development proposed. In addition, the impact on the Grade II listed barn at
 Burstead Grange has been assessed as causing less than substantial harm and is
 considered to be outweighed by the public benefits associated with the development.

1.8 Supporting technical assessments demonstrate that potential impacts relating to
 landscape, highways, flood risk, ecology, residential amenity and heritage can be
 appropriately mitigated and controlled through planning conditions and planning
 obligations. No statutory consultee has raised an objection that cannot be satisfactorily
 addressed through these mechanisms.

1.9 Having considered the proposal as a whole, and having regard to the presumption in
 favour of sustainable development contained within the Revised NPPF, Officers conclude
 that the benefits of the scheme, most notably the delivery of market and affordable
 housing, compliance with the Golden Rules and the provision of green infrastructure,
 significantly and demonstrably outweigh the identified harm.

1.10 Therefore, Officers are recommending approval of the application subject to the
 completion of a S106 Agreement and imposition of planning conditions as outlined in this
 report.

Minutes:
Councillor Blake and Councillor A Brown, having not been
present at the previous meeting, did not participate in discussion or vote on
this item.
Members were reminded that at the Planning Committee meeting
held on 7 October 2026 they had been minded to refuse planning permission for
Planning Application No. 25/01214/OUT. The report therefore returned to
Committee to seek agreement on the detailed wording of the reason for refusal.
RESOLVED:
That Planning Application No. 25/01214/OUT be refused
planning permission on the grounds that –
The proposed development constituted inappropriate
development within the Green Belt. It was considered that the application site
made a strong contribution to Green Belt purpose (a), as defined by Policy
GB2(1) of the NPPF, and therefore did not meet the definition of Grey Belt land
as set out in Policy GB7 (1) (g)(i). The proposed development would result in
substantial harm to the openness of the Green Belt and conflict with the
purposes of including land within the Green Belt. The Local Planning Authority
was not satisfied that the benefits of the scheme clearly outweighed the harm
to the Green Belt and other harm identified so as to amount to the very special
circumstances necessary to justify the development. The proposal was therefore
contrary to Section 13 of the NPPF, including Policies GB6 and GB7, and Saved
Policy BAS GB1.
VOTING –
For: 5, Against: 0, Abstained: 2

 including land within the Green Belt. The Local Planning Authority was not
 satisfied that the benefits of the scheme clearly outweighed the harm to the
 Green Belt and other harm identified so as to amount to the very special
 circumstances necessary to justify the development. The proposal was
 therefore contrary to Section 13 of the NPPF, including Policies GB6 and GB7,
 and Saved Policy BAS GB1.

[page 3]
GENERAL INFORMATION

Financial Implications

Local finance considerations are a matter to which local planning authorities are to
have regard in determining planning applications, as far as these are material to the
application. The New Homes Bonus (NHB) is capable of being a material
consideration to which the weight given shall be determined by the decision maker.

The New Homes Bonus is a payment to Local Authorities to match the Council tax of
net new dwellings built, paid by central Government over two consecutive years for
the period 2020/2021, reducing each year such that its weight may therefore diminish.

The development would generate a New Homes Bonus payment to Basildon Borough
Council.

Risk Management Implications

Risks associated with making decisions on planning applications relate to appeals,
cost awards and Judicial Review proceedings. The risks are managed as the Council
has adopted the national Code of Conduct and a specific code, ‘Probity in Planning’.
In addition, Members receive training in dealing with planning applications and Officer
advice is available at all stages of consideration of each application.

Opportunities associated with making decisions on planning applications relate to
making robust decisions in line with local and national planning policies which result
in sound planning decision making and increased public confidence in the planning
system.

Diversity, Inclusion and Community Cohesion Implications

As a public authority, Basildon Borough Council is subject to the requirement under
The Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED) found in s.149 of the Equality Act 2010 for the
council to have due regard to the need to:

a. Eliminate discrimination, harassment, victimisation and any other conduct
prohibited by the 2010 Act,
b. Advance equality of opportunity between persons who share a relevant protected
characteristic and those that do not, and
c. Foster good relations between persons who share a relevant protected
characteristic and those that do not.

The protected characteristics are: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and
civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual
orient

[page 4]
In this respect, the proposed development provides new market and affordable
housing which would provide modern properties improving the borough’s housing
stock. In terms of the relevant protected characteristics, it is considered that the
proposed development would help to positively contribute towards the requirements
of the Equality Act.

To inform Members that an application has been received from Mr Callum Muir of Little Bear

relates to the sale of alcohol for consumption both on and off the premises at The Little Bear
Bar, 7 High Street, Manningtree, Essex

have been received from a responsible authority and members of the public.


BACKGROUND

The application is made under the Licensing Act 2003 for the grant of a Premises Licence in
relation to the sale of alcohol both, on and off the premises.

The applicant has described The Little Bear Bar as the workshop space of 7 High Street,
Manningtree, which is located at the rear of the building. The primary access will be via North

From 12:00 New Years Eve until 01:00 New Years Day (indoors only from 21:00)

The full application can be found attached at Appendix A.

[page 2]
RELEVANT REPRESENTATIONS

Interested Parties/Other Persons

The Police Reform and Social Responsibility Act 2011 (PRSR Act 2011) removed from the
Licensing Act 2003 the specific reference for representations to be made by ‘interested parties’
and also removed the requirement that representations could only be accepted from persons
living in the ‘vicinity’ of the premises concerned, or who had for example, a business in the
‘vicinity’ of the premises.

There was no guidance or definition of ‘vicinity’ within the Licensing Act 2003 which effectively
had a limiting effect on those that could make relevant representations.

The PRSR Act 2011 replaced the references to ‘interested parties’ and ‘vicinity’ and substituted
that representations can be made and accepted by the Licensing Authority from ‘other persons’
which means that those persons do not necessarily have to live or run a business for
example in the proximity of the premises to be able to submit a valid and relevant
representation.

The relevant extracts from the Section 182 Guidance that accompanies the Licensing Act 2003
advises the following in relation to ‘other persons’. They are shown in italics for ease of
reference.

 8.12 As well as responsible authorities, any other person can play a role in a number of
 licensing processes under the 2003 Act. This includes any individual, body or business
 entitled to make representations to licensing authorities in relation to applications for the
 grant, variation, minor variation or review of premises licences and club premises
 certificates, regardless of their geographic proximity to the premises.

Representations can be made either against or in support of an application. The relevant
extracts from the Section 182 Guidance that accompanies the Licensing Act 2003 advises the
following in relation to this point.

 9.3 Relevant representations can be made in opposition to, or in support of, an
 application and can be made by any individual, body or business that has grounds to do
 so.

Nineteen representations/objections have been received from residents in relation to this
application.

The letters of objections can be found attached at Appendix B.

Responsi

[page 3]
FINANCE, OTHER RESOURCES AND RISK

A decision made by the Committee is subject to appeal at the Magistrates Court by the premises
user or a relevant person.


POLICY CONSIDERATIONS
The Licensing Act 2003 established a single integrated scheme for licensing premises that are
used for the supply of alcohol, regulated entertainment, or provision of late-night refreshment.
This system of licensing incorporates the sale of alcohol both on and off licensed premises;
public entertainment such as music, dancing, indoor sporting events, boxing or wrestling,
theatres, cinemas; and late-night refreshment houses and take-aways.

When determining the application with a view to promoting the licensing objectives in the overall
interests of the local community the Licensing Authority in the form of the Licensing Sub-
Committee must have regard and give appropriate weight to the following:

  Full Hearing Procedure for Applications for Premises Licences/Club Premises
 Certificates where representations have been received.
  Tendring District Council’s Statement of Licensing Policy -
 https://www.tendringdc.gov.uk/content/licensing-act-policy
  The Statutory Guidance issued by the Secretary of State under Section 182 of the
 Licensing Act 2003 - https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/explanatory-
 memorandum-revised-guidance-issued-under-s-182-of-licensing-act-2003
  The steps appropriate to positively promote the four ‘Licensing Objectives’.
  Representations (including supporting information) presented by all the parties.

Human Rights Implications

A Licence is to be regarded as the property of the applicant; however their right to the use of
the property must be balanced against all other public interests or representations in this matter
that the Premises/Personal Licences Sub-Committee may wish to consider as appropriate,
reasonable and proportionate in relation to the application that has been submitted and also
the representation/s that has/have been received against it.

In making their decision as to whether to grant this application, Members of the
Premises/Personal Licences Sub-Committee should also take into consideration Article 1 of the
First Protocol of 

[page 5]
RECOMMENDATION(S)

Each application must be considered in its own right and on its own merits only as to how it
might impact on the four licensing objectives which are the Prevention of Crime and Disorder,
the Prevention of Public Nuisance, Public Safety and the Protection of Children from Harm.

The Licensing Sub Committee is therefore asked to determine this application taking into
consideration the application in its own right and on its own merits and also all of the relevant
information that has been submitted as part of this report and at the hearing itself.

fieldwork. Members noted that the Cash and Bank review had received a
Substantial assurance opinion with only two low-priority recommendations,
whilst the follow-up review of IT Asset Management had achieved an Adequate assurance
opinion.
The Committee was advised that some audits had been removed
or deferred from the audit plan as a result of significant service developments

Head of Internal Audit's ability to provide an annual opinion at year-end.
Members noted progress in the implementation of audit

The Committee considered the Quarter 2 Treasury Management

Members were advised that the Capital and Investment
Strategy had been approved by Council as part of the budget-setting process in
February 2026 and provided the framework for the Council's treasury management,
capital financing and borrowing activities. It was reported that all treasury
management activities undertaken during the first six months of 2026/27 had
been carried out in accordance with the approved strategy and within the
Council's prudential indicators.
The Committee noted that total borrowing at the end of
Quarter 2 was £727 million, including finance leases, and that borrowing levels
had remained within the approved Capital Financing Requirement, Operational
Boundary and Authorised Limit throughout the period. Members also received an
update on capital expenditure, treasury management activity and performance
against prudential indicators.
During discussion, Members sought clarification regarding a
forecast underspend of £180,000 arising from the cessation of Area Committees.
Officers advised that, as no alternative scheme had currently been identified,
the amount remained a forecast underspend. It was noted that, should a decision
be taken to reintroduce Area Committees during the current financial year,
funding could potentially be made available from the existing budget provision.
The Committee also discussed the Council's investment
property in Dartford and its impact on borrowing levels. Members were advised
that the disposal process remained ongoing as negotiations had encountered
delays. It was reported that the Council remained committed to securing best
value from any sale and that a number of interested parties remained engaged.
The Leader of the Council advised that, given current borrowing levels, he did
not support any increase in the Council's long-term debt position and that
disposal of the Dartford asset should be progressed before consideration was
given to any further borrowing-funded investment opportunities.
Officers further clarified that short-term borrowing might
still be required for cash-flow management purposes, but that there was no
intention to increase the Council's Capital Financing Requirement or authorised
borrowing limits.
The Committee noted the Quarter 2 Treasury Management
update.

Management Practices laying down the policies, objectives and controls by which it will
conduct its treasury management activities. This report is based on the principles in
operation during 2026/27.

Treasury Management is defined in the Code of Practice as "the management of the
organisation’s cash flows, its banking, money market and capital market transactions; the
effective control of the risks associated with those activities and the pursuit of optimum
performance consistent with those risks."

[page 2]
The Council delegates all executive decisions on borrowing, investment and financing to
the Section 151 Officer who has responsibility for the proper administration of the
Council’s financial affairs. They in turn delegate the day-to-day treasury operations to
named staff within Finance and Commercial Services. Activities are further controlled
through Section 14 of the council’s Financial Regulations. In view of the complexity of
opportunities and options arising in the treasury management field, the Section 151 Officer
also employs the services of specialist consultants as advisers.

The Code of Practice for Treasury Management requires a minimum of three reports to
the Council on treasury management each year, as follows:

 • The Capital & Investment Strategy that the Section 151 Officer proposes for
 adoption for the year ahead (presented in February each year as part of the Budget
 Report);
 • A report after completion of the year comparing the actual treasury management

 approved for that year;
 • A mid-year report comparing the actual treasury management activity and the

With regard to the first requirement the Strategy for 2026/27 was considered by the Audit

treasury management updates are provided to the Audit and Risk Committee to support
ongoing oversight and scrutiny of treasury activities. This report provides the Quarter 2
Treasury Management Update for 2026/27 and covers the period from 1 April 2026 to 30
September 2026. A summary of treasury management performance and activity will also
be included within the quarterly Finance Update report to Cabinet, with the Quarter 2
Finance Update scheduled for consideration on 26 November 2026.

The Committee considered the Corporate Risk Management

Members were advised that the Council's risk management
framework was operating generally as intended, although further work was
required to improve the consistency, quality and timeliness of risk updates and
strengthen risk ownership across the organisation.
The Committee noted that the Council currently maintained 21

It was reported that mitigating actions were in place for
each of the red risks, although in many cases their effectiveness had not yet
been fully demonstrated and therefore continued to require close management
oversight. Members also noted a number of significant “amber” rated risks,
including Performance management, Information Governance, Partnerships, the
Housing C4 Recovery Programme and the Local Plan.
During discussion, Members raised concerns regarding cyber
security and the migration from legacy systems. Officers advised that the new
Housing Management System remained on track for implementation, that extensive
testing had been undertaken and that legacy systems would remain accessible
following go-live to mitigate implementation risks.
Members also queried the presentation of Local Plan risks
within the Corporate Risk Register in light of continuing Government
intervention. Officers acknowledged the potential disparity between risk
scoring and the position outlined elsewhere on the agenda and agreed to review the
assessment as part of the next reporting cycle.
The Committee discussed project governance arrangements and
concerns that some projects had historically progressed without full compliance
with project management requirements. Officers advised that a formal project
governance framework was now in place, including documented approval processes
and project management controls, and that action was being taken to ensure all
projects followed the required governance procedures before progressing into
delivery.
Members also discussed organisational culture, risk
ownership and the importance of ensuring appropriate accountability for the
implementation of recommendations and risk mitigation actions.

The system supports effective risk identification, assessment, monitoring and reporting,

Risk Management Policy, Strategy and Summary Toolkit

The Council has a Risk Management Policy, Strategy and Toolkit in place, which were
reviewed and approved by the Audit and Risk Committee in July 2026.

The Policy sets out the Council's risk management principles and risk appetite, recognising
that a degree of managed risk-taking is necessary to achieve the Council's objectives.
Accordingly, the Council adopts a cautious to open approach to risk, accepting risks where
decisions are informed, proportionate and supported by appropriate controls and mitigation
measures.

The Risk Management Strategy complements the Policy and supports the Council's wider
governance framework by setting out how risks will be managed, monitored and reported,
together with the key actions and activities required to further develop risk management
arrangements. The Strategy incorporates a Risk Management Action Plan to support
continuous improvement across the organisation.

The Policy and Strategy are supported by a Toolkit, which provides the framework,
methodology and processes for identifying, assessing, managing and reporting risks

Work is ongoing to embed the Council’s risk appetite across the organisation. Risk appetite
refers to the amount of risk the Council is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. This
does not mean that risks outside of these appetites cannot be taken; rather, when such risks

made with full awareness of potential impacts and benefits.

The aim is to establish clear boundaries for risk-taking and ensure that accepted risks are
proportionate to the potential rewards. Effective risk management should support informed
decision-making aligned with the Council’s risk appetite, build confidence in how risks are
responded to and provide transparency over the key risks faced and how they are managed.

attention remained, including governance compliance, the consistent application
of project and programme management arrangements, the timely provision of
information to support corporate processes, and engagement with assurance
activities such as internal audit.

implications of the continuing intervention and external oversight arrangements.

completion of agreed milestones rather than overall progress and therefore did
not necessarily represent the extent of work undertaken to date. Members also
discussed standards complaints and member conduct. Officers advised that, while
the number of complaints remained higher than desired, there had been
improvements in member conduct overall, evidenced by more orderly Council
meetings and a reduction in the number of councillors who were the subject of
repeated complaints. It was noted that a number of initiatives had been
undertaken to encourage improved standards and cross-party engagement, although
participation had been limited.

assessment of performance, improvement, risk and regulatory assurance.

Tenant Satisfaction Measures provide the golden thread through the report, connecting tenants’
experience with operational performance, complaints, service improvement, governance and
the evidence required by the Regulator of Social Housing. The report is therefore intended to
serve three connected audiences: tenants, who require clear and accessible information with
which to scrutinise their landlord; Cabinet, which requires consolidated evidence to support
oversight, challenge and decision-making; and the Regulator of Social Housing, which requires
robust evidence of compliance with the Consumer Standards.

Significant progress has been made during the year to strengthen governance, assurance and
regulatory compliance through completion of the Consumer Standards self-assessment,
implementation of the Housing Improvement and Delivery Plan, enhanced performance
monitoring arrangements and increased opportunities for tenant scrutiny and influence.

needs.

arrangements, improving customer satisfaction, implementing key transformation programmes,
embedding workforce changes and continuing delivery of the Housing Improvement and

rescue and rehoming organisations.

The Animal Activity Licensing Policy and Animal Charter have been developed to provide
a clear and comprehensive framework for the Council's animal licensing functions, while
reinforcing the Council's wider commitment to promoting and safeguarding high standards
of animal welfare across the Borough. The new Policy replaces the previous Animal
Welfare Charter and enhances the Council's approach to licensing, inspection and
enforcement activities, transparency in decision-making, partnership working and the
promotion of positive animal welfare outcomes.

The Policy and Charter were subsequently considered by Cabinet on 15 October 2026.
Having reviewed the report and the recommendations of the Licensing Committee,
Cabinet resolved to:

 1. Note the contents of the Animal Activity Licensing Policy and Animal Charter;

 2. Endorse the Policy as an important framework supporting animal welfare and
 regulatory best practice across the Borough; and

 3. Refer the Policy back to the Licensing Committee for final adoption.

The Policy has therefore now completed the Council's consultation and approval process.
Having previously considered the consultation findings and recommended the revised
document, and with Cabinet's endorsement now secured, the matter has been returned to
the Licensing Committee for final adoption of the Animal Activity Licensing Policy and
Animal Charter.

Revised Policy and Charter

The revised Animal Activity Licensing Policy and Animal Charter attached at Enclosure 1
incorporates all amendments arising from the consultation process and Licensing
Committee review.

To assist Members in its consideration of the document, all amendments have been
clearly highlighted in grey throughout the attached Policy and Charter.

The revised Policy and Charter will provide a clear framework for the Council's animal
licensing functions, support consistency in decision-making, strengthen transparency and
accountability and reaffirm the Council's commitment to promoting high standards of
animal welfare across the Borough.


LEGISLATION/POLICY

The relevant legislation does not directly require the Council to prepare and publish a
policy or consult. However, the dev

[page 3]
The Regulations allow for local authorities to charge a fee to carry out their duties under
the legislation. The animal licensing scheme falls within the definition of “services” and is
subject to the EU Services Directive, incorporated into UK law as the Provision of Services
Regulations 2009.


GENERAL INFORMATION

Financial Implications

The fees payable for specific premises / licences are dependent on the length of licence
granted, which is, in turn, dependent on the risk rating of the premises. In general, the
lower risk the premises is, the longer the licence will be granted for.

The animal licensing scheme falls within the definition of “services” and is subject to the
EU Services Directive, incorporated into UK law as the Provision of Services Regulations
2009.

Application fees are therefore split into two parts: Part A and Part B. Part A is the
application fee, which is payable on submission and covers the cost of considering and
processing the application. Part B is the licence fee, payable by successful applicants to
cover the costs of ongoing enforcement and compliance requirements.

Other potential financial considerations are for applicants/licensees in relation to the
issuing of Fixed Penalty Notices.

Risk Management Implications

Risks:

There is a risk that the Council’s reputation could be damaged if licensing policies are not
up to date and consistent with national guidance and standards.

The adoption of a policy reduces the risk of successful legal challenge. It is not a statutory
requirement for a Council to have an Animal Activity Licensing Policy and Animal Charter.
However, doing so has several benefits. For example, some of the decisions that the
Council may make will have a right of appeal against them and a policy will help to ensure
consistency and can be used to help justify any action that is taken.

Significant work has already been undertaken by the Licensing Team to secure
compliance amongst eligible operators, but work continues to identify illegal animal
activities.

Opportunities:

The approval of a policy will help to focus resources, especially around the receipt and
investigation of complaints.

The relevant legislatio

[page 4]
The policy creates transparency for all stakeholders outlining the manner in which the
Council intends to undertake its licensing responsibilities. The Policy outlines the Council’s
areas of responsibility and clarifies that non licensable animal activities fall outside its
remit. Additionally, the policy provides the Council with a basis for a robust defence to any
challenges that may be encountered in respect of decisions made and enforcement action
taken.

The development and regular review of a policy will ensure that the Council satisfies its
legal responsibilities with respect to specific elements of the Regulators’ Code and will
assist the Council in demonstrating that it has had due regard to the Code in relation to
this particular area of law.



Diversity, Inclusion and Community Cohesion Implications

As a public authority, Basildon Borough Council is subject to the requirement under The
Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED) found in s.149 of the Equality Act 2010 for the council
to have due regard to the need to:

 a. Eliminate discrimination, harassment, victimisation and any other conduct
 prohibited by the 2010 Act

 b. Advance equality of opportunity between persons who share a relevant protected
 characteristic and those that do not, and

 c. Foster good relations between persons who share a relevant protected
 characteristic and those that do not.


The protected characteristics are: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil
partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation.

The implementation and enforcing of Animal Activity Licensing Policy and Animal Charter
will be in accordance with the Equality Act 2010. There will be no discriminatory
enforcement of this proposal in line with our PSED.

An EIA will be completed to consider how the proposed changes within the Animal Activity
Licensing Policy and Animal Charter might adversely or positively impact those persons
with protected characteristics. It will consider the PSED and also the impact of the
proposed changes on human rights and wider non-legislative factors.

Basildon residents are set to lose an important democratic
safeguard when changes to the National Scheme of Delegation come into force on
31 October.
These
changes will significantly reduce the ability of elected councillors to ensure
that contentious planning applications are considered publicly by a committee
of elected representatives, instead placing greater decision-making power in
the hands of unelected officials.
This
Council believes that major or contentious planning decisions affecting local
communities should remain subject to meaningful democratic scrutiny.

Condemns the Government’s decision to weaken the role of locally elected
councillors in the planning process and reduce the democratic voice of Basildon
residents.
*
Calls on the Leader of Basildon Council to write to the Government demanding
that implementation of the National Scheme of Delegation is halted and that
Ministers urgently reconsider reforms which remove important local democratic
safeguards.
*
Calls on the Government to ensure that residents continue to have a meaningful
route through their elected representatives to have contentious planning
applications considered publicly and democratically.

Service Spending
This Council believes that residents
should be able to see clearly how public money is spent across every part of
the borough.
For too long, residents have been
unable to get a clear, regular picture of how spending on visible neighbourhood

parks maintenance and street cleansing affect people’s daily lives, and spending

the
amount spent;
that
ward’s percentage of the service’s total borough-wide spend;
the
service’s total monthly and year-to-date spend; and
a
breakdown, where available, between staffing, contractors, materials and
other costs.

spending that cannot be directly assigned to a ward, such as shared staff,
equipment or borough-wide contracts, to be apportioned using a clear and
consistent method, with that method explained in the report.

written public explanation whenever spending is substantially concentrated
in one ward, or when a ward’s share changes substantially from the
previous month. The explanation must set out the reason for the spending
and whether it reflects planned work, urgent need or another factor.

the reports to be published on the Council’s website within 30 days of
each month end, with the first report covering the earliest period for
which reliable information is available.

the Chief Executive to ensure that the reporting process is implemented
within 28 days of this resolution and that reports continue to be
published monthly. Reports backdating to May 2024 will also be published
for historical context.

BASILDON BOROUGH COUNCIL


Report to: Finance, Procurement & Efficiency Scrutiny Committee

 Q2 BUDGET MONITORING AND MEDIUM TERM FINANCIAL STRATEGY UPDATE –
 GENERAL FUND & HOUSING REVENUE ACCOUNT 2026/27


Report by: Leader of the Council, Cabinet Member for Finance & Strategy

Supported by: Assistant Director of Finance & Governance

Enquiries to: Andrew Wilks, Finance Manager (Management Accounting),
 andrew.wilks@basildon.gov.uk

Enclosures: Enclosure No. 1 – Budget Monitoring Detail by Portfolio


EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

This report presents the forecast outturn for 2026/27, at the end of September 2026 (Quarter
2).

The overall summary position for the General Fund is a projected overspend of £3.8m. This
projected overspend has increased by £0.4m since Quarter 1. One of the key contributing
factors continues to be temporary accommodation to cover our statutory duty around
homelessness and more specifically the availability of alternative accommodation to reduce
the need to use expensive nightly paid accommodation. There are other cost pressures
related to capital financing, staffing and risk of savings non-delivery. These are partly offset
by additional planning income.

The overall summary position for the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) is a projected
overspend of £3.2m. This is an improvement of £1.3m since Quarter 1. This continues to
be due to the significant rise in repair costs, dealing with damp and mould cases, as well as
additional costs associated with delivering against the requirements of the Regulatory
Notice issued by the Regulator for Social Housing.

The full financial position is summarised within the report, with specific focus and detail on
the key contributing factors and the actions being taken to mitigate against them. To the
extent that any pressures are unable to be managed by the end of the financial year, the
Council will need to apply revenue reserves to balance the budget. The detailed breakdown
of all services can be found in Enclosure No. 1.

The information contained within this report is a key input to the Council’s Medium Term
Financial Strategy (MTFS). Emerging issues, risks and financial pressures identifie

[page 2]
Members are asked to review the report and provide observations on the projected outturn
position, including any significant variances and their implications for the delivery of key
service objectives within the Council's Corporate Plan. Any comments arising from this
review will be taken into account ahead of the report being presented to Cabinet on 26
November.

_______________________________________________________________________

BACKGROUND

Budget monitoring is a vital component of the Council’s financial management framework,
supporting effective decision making, informing the year end closure process and
contributing to the ongoing development of the Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS). It
plays a key role in maintaining strong financial governance and ensuring the Council’s long-
term financial sustainability.

The timely identification of budget variances, emerging pressures and financial risks
enables appropriate corrective action and mitigating measures to be implemented, helping
to safeguard the delivery essential services and support the achievement of the Council’s
Corporate Plan objectives.

In addition, a number of the variances identified through budget monitoring are expected to
have ongoing financial implications beyond the current year. As a result, these issues will
inform future budget setting decisions and contribute to the development of the MTFS.

The 2026/27 General Fund approved budget identified a MTFS budget gap of £5.8m in
2027/28, rising to £13.1m by 2029/30. The variances and pressures identified within this
report may have implications for the Council’s medium term position and could affect the
projected gap. These impacts will continue to be assessed alongside mitigating actions and
other factors as the MTFS

[page 3]
will be reported to Members as appropriate, and any overspend remaining at the year-end
will need to be met from reserves.

Please note that the monitoring position of the capital programme is reported separately
through the Capital & Investment Strategy quarterly reports presented to Audit & Risk
Committee. The Cabinet report consolidates these positions into a single report to provide
a more comprehensive overview.

REPORT of
DIRECTOR OF PLACE, PLANNING AND GROWTH
to
COUNCIL (EXTRAORDINARY)
11 NOVEMBER 2026

MALDON DISTRICT LOCAL PLAN 2040 - REGULATION 20 SCOPING DOCUMENT

1. PURPOSE OF THE REPORT

1.1 For the Council to agree and publish the Regulation (Reg) 20 Scoping Document for
 the Maldon District Local Plan 2040. This notification will provide key stakeholders
 (general and specific consulting bodies) and the local community with the opportunity
 to comment before the start of the plan making process. The focus of this document
 is on what should be included in a future Local Plan and how we should engage
 during future consultations.


2. RECOMMENDATIONS

 That the Council:

 (i) agrees the content of the Reg 20 Scoping Document for the Maldon District
 Local Plan 2040 and the associated questions (APPENDIX 1) for public
 engagement between 25 November 2026 until its closing date on 22
 December 2026;

 (ii) delegates authority to the Director of Place, Planning and Growth, in
 consultation with of the Chairperson of the Planning Policy Working Group to
 make minor changes to the content and format the Reg 20 Scoping
 Document (APPENDIX 1) prior to the start of the scoping.


3. SUMMARY OF KEY ISSUES

3.1 Background

3.1.1 An earlier version of the Scoping Document was considered by the Planning Policy
 Working Group (PPWG) on Thursday 8 October 2026. An all-Member briefing on the
 Document was also held on 27 October 2026. Amendments have been made
 following engagement with Members.

3.1.2 On 10 September 2026, Council members agreed to commence work on the Maldon
 District Local Plan under the new 30-month plan-making system. The timetable for
 the Local Plan was also agreed and included the dates for the commencement of the
 Reg 20 Scoping, notifying key stakeholders of the Council’s intention to start a new
 Local Plan.

[page 2]
3.1.3 Preparatory work on the new Local Plan formally commenced on 25 September 2026
 when the Council published the Notice of Intention to Commence Plan Making and
 the associated Timetable on the Council’s website:
 www.maldon.gov.uk/newlocalplan. The publication of these documents marked the
 start of the required four-month period prior to Gateway 1.

3.1.4 Gateway 1 is the first of three mandatory Gateways that the Council needs to pass
 through as it prepares a new Local Plan. Gateway 1 requires the Council to publish a
 self-assessment summary demonstrating its readiness to start the formal 30-month
 local plan process. It is intended that the Gateway 1 self-assessment summary will
 be published on 13 March 2027. The Council then has 24 months to prepare the plan
 and undertake consultations prior to submitting the plan for examination, with
 adoption taking place in month 30.

3.1.5 Before the Council publishes its Gateway 1 self-assessment, it needs to be making
 progress in the five areas set out in the regulations:
  prepare and publish a local plan timetable (this has been completed and was
 published on 25 September 2026)
  establish project management and governance arrangements about the
 preparation of the plan (this has been completed as part of the PID [Project
 Initiation Document] agreed at Council on 10 September)
  establish the Council’s approach to consulting and engaging on the Local
 Plan (this will be informed by responses to the Scoping Document)
  anticipated content of the Local Plan (this will be informed by responses to
 the Scoping Document)
  progressing the Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA) (this will begin to
 be informed by responses to the Scoping Document)

3.2 Scoping Document Requirements

3.2.1 The next step in the plan-making process is the publication of the Regulation 20
 Scoping Document. This report to the Council is seeking Members consideration of
 the contents and publication of the Scoping Document.

3.2.2 The Scoping Document must commence after the publication of the Notice of
 Intention to Commence Plan-Making and Timetable and will inform the Gateway 1
 self-assessment.

[page 3]
3.2.3 The Scoping Document provides the local community and other key stakeholders
 with the opportunity to have their say at the start of the plan-making process. The
 Council must ask for views on:
  what to include in the Local Plan,
  how to approach future Local Plan engagement, and
  any other matter which the Council wants to consult on.

3.2.4 During this notification the Council must invite representations from:
  general consultation bodies the Council considers appropriate, and
  specific consultation bodies the Council considers may have an interest in the
 preparation of the Local Plan.

3.2.5 These consultation bodies are specified within the plan-making regulations 2026. The
 Council does not have to invite anyone else, but anyone can make representations at
 this stage.

3.2.6 The Scoping Document will run between the 25 November and 22 December 2026,
 as detailed within the published timetable, as agreed at Council on 10 September.

3.3 Proposed Scoping Document

3.3.1 The draft Scoping Document is attached at APPENDIX 1. As set out in paragraph
 3.3.3 of this report, the Government’s requirements for a Reg 20 Scoping are high-
 level. The proposed Scoping Document has therefore been prepared to provide an
 appropriate level of detail on the key matters to be considered, while remaining
 proportionate to this early stage of plan preparation. The content is considered to
 accord with the Government’s requirements. More detailed consultation on the
 proposed content of the Local Plan will be undertaken at the future stages of plan
 preparation (August 2027: consultation on the proposed plan content and evidence
 and May 2028: consultation on the proposed local plan).

3.3.2 The previous work and consultations undertaken to inform the Local Development
 Plan review have been feeding into the Scoping Document and the emerging work on
 the Local Plan.

3.3.3 The new plan must be consistent with national planning policy. The National Planning
 Policy Framework (NPPF) 2026 was published on 17 August 2026 and contains plan-
 making policies which the plan will need to accord with. The NPPF also contains
 national decision-making policies (sometimes

[page 4]
3.5 Amendments to Scoping Document wording

3.5.1 Due to the tight time frames, it is important that minor changes can be made to the
 Scoping Document and formatting to ensure deadlines are met. Minor adjustments to
 wording and formatting may be required when adapting the content for an online
 survey to ensure it is suitable for digital presentation. To reassure Members, a minor
 change is a change which does not alter the underlying policy intent, legal effect,
 substantive rights, responsibilities, powers or decision-making arrangements set out
 in the document.


4. CONCLUSION

4.1 The proposed Scoping Document is consistent with Government requirements and
 will place the Council in a position to publish its Gateway 1 self-assessment summary
 in early 2027, while maintaining alignment with the agreed and published timetable.


5. IMPACT ON PRIORITIES AS SET OUT IN THE CORPORATE PLAN 2025 – 2028

5.1 The Scoping Document is a key milestone in the process of the preparation of the
 Maldon District Local Plan 2040.

5.2 Supporting our communities

5.2.1 The Corporate Plan highlights that the district needs more homes to meet the
 demand of our growing population and government targets, including affordable
 homes and temporary housing. Developing a new Local Plan will contribute towards
 these priorities.

5.3 Investing in our District

5.3.1 The Corporate Plan identifies that the Council is seeking to provide a better place for
 residents, businesses and visitors, ensures the right development is in the right
 places, and delivery of well-designed housing and healthy places. Developing a new
 Local Plan will contribute towards these priorities.

5.4 Growing our economy

5.4.1 The Government links the delivery of new homes to the need to support the
 economy. The housing sector provides jobs within the district and assists in
 supporting the local and national economy. A new Local Plan will support the delivery
 of new homes as well as economic growth opportunities.

5.5 Protecting our environment

5.5.1 A new Local Plan will contain policies to support the protection of our environment
 and mitigate the environmental impact of new developments.

5.6 Deliver

[page 5]
6. IMPLICATIONS

 (i) Impact on Customers – Working on a new Local Plan benefits customers by
 shaping future development to create well-connected, sustainable
 communities with improved local services and amenities.

 (ii) Impact on Equalities – There are no direct impact upon equalities arising
 from the recommendations in this report. An Equalities Impact Assessment
 will be undertaken as part of the new Local Plan.

 (iii) Impact on Risk (including Fraud implications) – There are no direct risks
 arising from the recommendations in this report. The funding for the plan was
 agreed at Council on 10 September 2026.

 (iv) Impact on Resources (financial) – There is no direct impact on resources
 (financial) arising from the recommendations in this report.

 (v) Impact on Resources (human) – There is no direct impact on resources
 (financial) arising from the recommendations in this report.

 (vi) Impact on Devolution / Local Government Reorganisation – There are no
 direct impacts on Devolution or Local Government Reorganisation (LGR)
 arising from the recommendations in this report. The Government is
 encouraging Councils to continue to progress Local Plans despite the
 decision to pause and review LGR. A new Maldon District Local Plan will
 provide a legacy for the district.

Budget monitoring is a vital component of the Council’s financial management framework,
supporting effective decision making, informing the year end closure process and
contributing to the ongoing development of the Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS). It
plays a key role in maintaining strong financial governance and ensuring the Council’s long-
term financial sustainability.

The timely identification of budget variances, emerging pressures and financial risks
enables appropriate corrective action and mitigating measures to be implemented, helping
to safeguard the delivery essential services and support the achievement of the Council’s
Corporate Plan objectives.

In addition, a number of the variances identified through budget monitoring are expected to
have ongoing financial implications beyond the current year. As a result, these issues will
inform future budget setting decisions and contribute to the development of the MTFS.

The 2026/27 General Fund approved budget identified a MTFS budget gap of £5.8m in
